title: A Later Expedition, a Different Stage
imageAlt: Selected sequence: Legazpi's expedition departed Mexico in 1564, crossed the Pacific, and established a Spanish settlement in Cebu in 1565. Departure and arrival are distinct events.
content:
Chapter 5 ended with later voyages and a question: when does a visit become an attempt to maintain colonial rule? Chapter 6 begins with Miguel Lopez de Legazpi's expedition. This was a later journey, not Magellan's fleet returning under a different name.

Legazpi's expedition departed from Mexico, then part of New Spain, in 1564. It crossed the Pacific and reached the Philippine islands in 1565. After visiting several places, it established a Spanish settlement in Cebu that year. Existing communities and their histories were already there.

Watch how to read the timeline. First identify what the date labels: departure or a later event. Next connect the places in a selected sequence. Finally state a limit: the line omits many stops and does not show exact sailing directions, distance or everyone's experience.

Compare this with your earlier work. Magellan died in 1521; Legazpi's 1564-1565 expedition was much later. Keep leaders, journeys and events separate before explaining how the colonial presence developed.
clues: Read the departure
Legazpi's expedition left Mexico in 1564. A departure year is not automatically an arrival year.
Read the later event
The expedition reached the Philippine islands and established a Spanish settlement in Cebu in 1565.
Keep journeys separate
Legazpi's expedition was distinct from Magellan's earlier voyage and from Elcano's return.
task: Which report keeps the expedition sequence clear?
Legazpi's expedition departed Mexico in 1564 and established a Spanish settlement in Cebu in 1565
Legazpi and Magellan commanded one fleet in 1521
The departure from Mexico and all arrivals happened on the same day
Cebu had no people or history before 1565
reason: Legazpi's 1564 departure and the 1565 Cebu settlement belong to a later expedition, distinct from Magellan's voyage.
definition: An organized journey with a particular purpose.

title: Aims and Different Responsibilities
imageAlt: A comparison guide distinguishes Spanish aims of occupation and a return connection, Legazpi's command, and Urdaneta's navigation knowledge. It does not credit one person with every task.
content:
A voyage has aims and people with different responsibilities. The Spanish Crown sought to occupy the islands and establish a continuing presence. A workable return connection across the Pacific also mattered. These were the sponsor's aims, not proof that communities had accepted them.

Legazpi commanded the expedition. Andres de Urdaneta, an Augustinian friar with earlier Pacific experience, contributed navigation knowledge and helped with the return route. A friar is a member of a religious community. We study his role as history; students are not asked to adopt his religion.

Try a fictional team-record task. One card describes command, another describes navigation knowledge, and a third describes the sponsor's aims. Put each in the right column. Do not give a single person credit for every action by the crews or erase the people who already lived at the destinations.

An aim tells what was wanted. A responsibility tells who undertook a task. An outcome tells what happened. Keeping these separate helps you evaluate the expedition rather than assume every plan succeeded.
clues: An imperial aim
Occupation and a continuing presence were Spanish aims. A sponsor's plan is different from local agreement.
Different roles
Legazpi commanded; Urdaneta contributed navigation knowledge. Crews and other participants also mattered.
A result to investigate
An instruction or responsibility does not prove that every aim was achieved everywhere.
task: Which comparison correctly separates roles and aims?
Legazpi commanded, Urdaneta contributed navigation knowledge, and Spanish aims did not establish local consent
Urdaneta's religious role meant all residents shared his beliefs
One leader performed every task without a crew
A sponsor's instruction proved every community agreed
reason: Command, navigation knowledge and Spanish aims were distinct. Plans and responsibilities do not establish universal consent or success.
definition: A task or duty a person is expected to carry out.

title: Local Responses Were Part of the Story
imageAlt: Three evidence questions ask what action was recorded, who took part, and what remains unknown. Force, resistance and agreements must not be turned into one response from everyone.
content:
The expedition arrived among communities with their own leaders and interests. Local people could negotiate, provide supplies or resist. An account about the newcomers alone cannot explain the whole encounter.

Establishing the Spanish presence in Cebu involved force and local opposition, not simply an invitation from every resident. A historical marker in Cebu also records an agreement between Rajah Tupas and Legazpi in 1565. A later agreement and earlier conflict can both be part of the history. Do not turn either into the feelings of every individual.

Read a fictional exhibit claim: One recorded agreement proves everyone freely supported the whole colonial project. Check the leap. Who participated? What did the agreement address? What pressure or conflict surrounded it? More evidence is needed for a statement about all residents.

A treaty record can help explain a formal relationship. It cannot reveal every private motive or stand for every community in the archipelago. Name local participants and distinguish a recorded action from an unsupported claim of universal consent.
clues: A conflict to acknowledge
The Spanish settlement in Cebu involved force and local opposition. Do not describe it as a welcome from everyone.
A recorded agreement
The Cebu marker records an agreement between Rajah Tupas and Legazpi in 1565.
A limit on interpretation
An agreement involving named leaders does not by itself reveal every person's wishes or represent every island.
task: Which report uses the local-response evidence carefully?
Cebu's history included conflict and a recorded agreement; neither establishes everyone's wishes
All residents welcomed every Spanish demand without pressure
No local leader made any decision
One agreement proves every island accepted colonial rule
reason: Local opposition, force and a recorded agreement all belong in the account. A leader's agreement is not proof of everyone's consent.
definition: Discussion between people or groups trying to reach an agreement.

title: A Settlement Within an Existing Community
imageAlt: A comparison distinguishes arrival, maintaining a settlement and claiming authority. A Spanish settlement in Cebu did not create Cebu's existing community or establish immediate control everywhere.
content:
A settlement is a place where people establish a continuing base to live. The Spanish settlement in Cebu in 1565 differed from a brief visit. Maintaining that presence required supplies, organization and relationships with people in the region.

This did not mean Legazpi created Cebu. Its trading community and local leadership existed before the expedition. Use precise wording: a Spanish settlement was established in an already inhabited place. Saying Cebu began in 1565 would erase earlier history.

Work through a fictional evidence table. A ship arriving supports a claim of arrival. Records of a maintained base support a claim of continuing presence there. Neither alone proves effective authority over every island. To investigate that larger claim, ask where institutions operated, how people responded and what limits remained.

The next missions examine settlements in Cebu and Manila and the expansion of colonial control. Here, explain the first step without jumping to the end: one settlement mattered, but colonial rule developed unevenly and did not become universal on a single day.
clues: More than a visit
A maintained settlement is evidence of a continuing presence, different from a ship's brief arrival.
An existing place
Cebu already had a community, trade and leadership. The Spanish settlement did not create its entire history.
Check the reach
A settlement in one place does not establish immediate, effective control over every island.
task: Which sentence describes the 1565 settlement precisely?
A Spanish base was established in existing Cebu; its presence did not prove control of every island
Legazpi created Cebu and all its earlier history
One settlement immediately governed every community
A settlement is always only a ship passing offshore
reason: The Spanish base was a continuing presence within an existing community. Its establishment was not proof of instant control everywhere.
definition: A place where people establish a continuing base to live.

title: Why a Return Route Mattered
imageAlt: Selected sequence connects a 1564 departure, the 1565 Cebu base and a return voyage to Mexico in 1565. It is not a geographic map or a complete trade history.
content:
Reaching the islands did not answer every question about staying connected across the Pacific. A return route mattered for carrying news, people and supplies. Trade also depended on continuing connections, not just one arrival.

In 1565, the San Pedro made a return voyage from Cebu to Mexico. Urdaneta contributed navigation knowledge, while Felipe de Salcedo captained the ship and other navigators and crew carried out the journey. Winds and currents helped shape the route. The journey was a team effort, not one person sailing alone.

The return is often discussed as the tornaviaje. We use that word here for the return journey. Do not turn it into a claim that no other person ever attempted or completed a Pacific crossing. This scene does not settle every question about priority among voyages.

Use the diagram as a sequence, not sailing directions. Then explain a connection: a workable return could help support communication and continued presence. It did not guarantee safety on every voyage, erase local resistance or by itself prove control across the archipelago.
clues: A connection
A return route could carry news, people and supplies between the islands and Mexico.
Shared work
The 1565 San Pedro return involved Urdaneta, captain Felipe de Salcedo, navigators and crew.
A limit
A workable route did not make every voyage safe or establish control of every community.
task: Why did a workable return connection matter to the expedition's continuing presence?
It could support communication and supplies without guaranteeing safety or control everywhere
It proved every local community had consented
It made winds and currents irrelevant
It meant one navigator performed the whole journey alone
reason: The return connection helped communication and supplies. Navigation and crew work mattered, but a route did not guarantee safety or universal control.
definition: A return journey; here, the voyage back across the Pacific to Mexico.

title: Your Expedition Evidence Report
imageAlt: A report guide asks learners to connect a dated event, evidence of an action and a limit. It does not treat an expedition's account as everyone's viewpoint.
content:
Build an explanation that connects the expedition with the beginning of a continuing Spanish presence. Keep the 1564 departure and the events of 1565 distinct. Separate Legazpi's command from Urdaneta's navigation work and the work of other participants.

Include local responses. Conflict, pressure and an agreement with named leaders cannot be reduced to one opinion held by every resident. Describe the settlement as a Spanish base in an existing community, and connect the return journey with communication and supplies.

Use this classroom report frame in your own words: The expedition aimed to [aim]. At [place and year], the evidence shows [action]. Local responses included [supported response]. The return connection mattered because [reason]. We should not claim [unsupported conclusion]. This frame is not an original quotation.

Use the mission quiz to check what you learned. If a topic is difficult, revisit its lesson and try targeted practice before another quiz attempt. Passing earns the mission reward once. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: Connect the events
Distinguish departure, settlement and the return journey rather than using one date for everything.
Include participants
Local people, expedition leaders, navigators and crew had different roles and interests.
State the limit
A participant's account or a leader's agreement cannot establish every resident's thoughts or universal control.
task: Which final report best fits the mission evidence?
A later expedition established a Spanish base amid local responses, while a return connection supported continued contact
Legazpi created Cebu's history and every person agreed
One arrival immediately gave effective control over all islands
One person performed every voyage role without any crew
reason: Connect chronology, different roles, local responses, settlement and the return route while keeping the limits of the evidence clear.
definition: An explanation that links claims with sources and identifies what the evidence does not establish.
